{"id": "53:25/q01", "question": "What do 'the later' and 'the first' denote here?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "53:25/q01/p1", "position": "The afterlife and this worldly life, including what each contains.", "reasons": "Rāzī says al-ākhirah qualifies an understood 'life' or 'abode.' Ibn ʿAṭiyyah calls them two abodes. Farrāʾ includes the reward of each; Ibn ʿĀshūr says their contents are included and compares the two easts and wests of 55:17. Elmalılı calls them the first and final stages of human life."}]}
{"id": "53:25/q02", "question": "How is ٱلْءَاخِرَةُ related to the form and sense of 'last'?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "53:25/q02/p1", "position": "It is the feminine of 'last,' whose apparent active participle has no attested simple verb and denotes true finality.", "reasons": "Rāzī illustrates a hypothetical base by أخرته فتأخر but says usage does not establish the expected form. He explains that completed pastness would need a true endpoint, while تأخر can express a reflexive effort or claim to being last. He treats آخر as a participial form intensified as أفعل; he distinguishes a connected final part from the separate thing that comes after it."}]}
{"id": "53:25/q03", "question": "How is ٱلْأُولَىٰ formed and inflected?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "53:25/q03/p1", "position": "It is the feminine فعلى of أول, an exceptional أفعل form; Arabic also has أولة, accounting for different inflection.", "reasons": "Rāzī says every أفعل/فعلى pair calls for a base, though the base here is unattested. أول has neither a verb nor a participle: an agent precedes its act, so an act cannot make the first thing first. His reply to سبق/سابق treats 'preceder' as resemblance rather than derivation; تقدم is answered through his discussion of تأخر. He rejects derivation from آل ('making another first') as far-fetched. Arabs use both أولة and أولى, the latter more common and the Qurʾanic form; أولة permits tanwin while أولى is diptote, explaining أولا with or without tanwin. He calls أولة etymological but weaker. He also reports a proposal that أفعل is diptote only if its feminine is exclusively فعلى; a ة feminine would remove that condition."}]}
{"id": "53:25/q04", "question": "How do 'first' and 'last' differ from 'before' and 'after'?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "53:25/q04/p1", "position": "First and last express endpoints, whereas before and after express a wider relation.", "reasons": "Rāzī says أول and آخر have أفعل/فاعل morphology unlike قبل and بعد. آخر demands an afterness beyond which nothing follows; something after the first may still be intermediate. Arriving after everyone explains being last, but being last does not explain every use of 'after.'"}]}
{"id": "53:25/q05", "question": "What does placing 'for God' first convey?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "53:25/q05/p1", "position": "It marks God's exclusive ownership of the two lives.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr says the fronting makes explicit the further restriction implied by the previous verse, 53:24: the two lives belong to God rather than people. Qushayrī describes His sovereignty as complete and creatures as deficient; Ṭabāṭabāʾī denies any partner in either dominion."}]}
{"id": "53:25/q06", "question": "Why is the afterlife mentioned before this life?", "turns_on": "Whether the ordering is primarily semantic, primarily a verse-ending choice, or serves both; Biqāʿī disputes the rhyme explanation.", "positions": [{"id": "53:25/q06/p1", "position": "To give the afterlife priority because the argument centers on hopes or consequences there.", "reasons": "Biqāʿī says pleasures, attained wishes, and deprivation come to full realization there, where idolaters expect their gods to secure prosperity; only followers of guidance who resist desire attain their wishes there, while nobody gets every worldly wish. He explicitly says the order is semantic because al-ukhrā could also have supplied the rhyme. Ālūsī stresses rebutting opponents' hope of winning in the afterlife, which leads into the next verse."}, {"id": "53:25/q06/p2", "position": "To preserve the verse ending.", "reasons": "Itqān calls the order reversed for the verse ending and compares 'We gathered you and the earlier peoples' in 77:38. Biqāʿī argues against rhyme as the explanation, observing that al-ukhrā would also rhyme."}, {"id": "53:25/q06/p3", "position": "Both to emphasize the later life and to fit the verse ending.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥayyān says the afterlife comes later chronologically and that the ending fits, comparing 92:13. Ibn ʿĀshūr says the order directs believers' concern toward the more important afterlife while fitting the ending."}]}
{"id": "53:25/q07", "question": "What does God's ownership of both lives entail?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "53:25/q07/p1", "position": "God alone owns and governs both worlds; what anyone receives or does there depends on His will and permission.", "reasons": "Muqātil relates this to resurrection and recompense (6:12; 53:31). Farrāʾ includes rewards. Naḥḥās, Thaʿlabī, Kashshāf, Qurṭubī, Bayḍāwī, and Abū Ḥayyān emphasize God's granting or withholding as He wills. Qushayrī adds that He creates both and has complete sovereignty while creatures lack it. Wāḥidī's Basīṭ and Baghawī say nobody possesses anything without permission; Wāḥidī's Wajīz and Ibn Kathīr say nothing occurs contrary to His will. Ibn ʿAṭiyyah adds power and authority; Nasafī adds His governance. Biqāʿī calls the entire dominion His; Elmalılı says human life begins by His will and the afterlife proceeds under His law. Ibn ʿĀshūr applies His governance to each world's inhabitants. Ṭabāṭabāʾī excludes a partner; Study Quran says pagans' conjectural picture effectively denies this mastery."}]}
{"id": "53:25/q08", "question": "Does a person's wish determine what they receive in either life?", "turns_on": "The explanations stress sovereign allocation, beneficial gifts to deserving believers, or recompense by deeds; Jishumī prefers Abū ʿAlī's more comprehensive account.", "positions": [{"id": "53:25/q08/p1", "position": "No; God grants or withholds according to His will and permission, so wishes alone secure nothing.", "reasons": "Wāḥidī's Basīṭ explicitly rebuts the unbeliever's wish. Kashshāf and Bayḍāwī say no one may dictate to God; Qurṭubī and Abū Ḥayyān similarly set His will above desire. Biqāʿī cites the returning person's false hope for good in 41:50 as proof of subjection to the sole sovereign. Bursevī and Ṭabāṭabāʾī make ownership the reason wishes are not guaranteed. Ālūsī calls this an explanation of the previous denial. Islahi says the question of wishes expresses amazement at the preceding argument, while desire cannot replace truth or override divine law. Ibn ʿĀshūr says the clause adds the restriction implicit in 53:24."}, {"id": "53:25/q08/p2", "position": "God gives beneficial worldly and otherworldly goods, but afterlife success belongs to deserving believers.", "reasons": "Abū ʿAlī names religion, wealth, prophethood, and Paradise among the possible benefits; Jishumī explicitly prefers this comprehensive reading. Elmalılı says final good requires following revealed proof and rules, with practical grounding rather than bare ideals. Biqāʿī says followers of guidance who resist desire attain their wishes in the afterlife, unlike idolaters expecting intercession; worldly wishes are never all fulfilled."}, {"id": "53:25/q08/p3", "position": "No; deeds are recompensed, so wishing does not cancel reward or punishment.", "reasons": "Jishumī reports this as another explanation: God rewards obedience and punishes disobedience. Rāzī reports punishment in this life or the next for one who chooses a desired deity and cites 53:26 against hoped-for intercession. Islahi says false hopes collapse when judgment follows the balance of good and evil deeds, ending in Paradise or Hell; he also says conjecture cannot defeat real reward and punishment. Muqātil links ownership to resurrection and recompense (6:12; 53:31)."}]}
{"id": "53:25/q09", "question": "What does the verse imply about intercession?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "53:25/q09/p1", "position": "Intercession is subject to God's permission and acceptance; idols and other beings cannot provide it independently.", "reasons": "Muqātil places the declaration after people hoped angels would intercede. Nasafī says God grants intercession only to whom He wills and approves. Rāzī says 53:26 answers the claim that al-Lāt and al-ʿUzzā are angelic intercessors; the idols rest on conjecture and desire. Ibn ʿĀshūr cites the idolaters' claims in 39:3 and 10:18, arguing even honored angels need God's leave and acceptance for a recipient, while earthly stone idols have still less claim. He says the transition makes the gravity of intercession clear. Islahi and Kur'an Yolu also deny independent intercession or change to God's decisions. Asad says omnipotence and omniscience leave God in need of no mediator."}]}
{"id": "53:25/q10", "question": "What does this ownership imply for prophethood and guidance?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "53:25/q10/p1", "position": "God gives prophethood and guidance to those He chooses, rather than to anyone who wishes for them.", "reasons": "Māwardī grounds God's choice of prophet in His ownership of heaven and earth. Nasafī includes prophethood among grants by divine will and approval. Rāzī reports an answer to unbelievers who inferred believers' inferior guidance from their lack of wealth: God distributes both wealth and guidance as He wills, citing 46:11. Abū ʿAlī includes religion and prophethood among beneficial gifts. Kur'an Yolu reports Ṭabarī's view that Muhammad's high rank came by grace rather than his wish."}]}

{"id": "53:25/q12", "question": "How does the verse connect to the surrounding argument?", "turns_on": "Rāzī offers several contextual readings: idol worship and intercession, punishment, consolation, proof of resurrection, and the wealth objection.", "positions": [{"id": "53:25/q12/p1", "position": "It answers wishes grounded in idols, conjecture, and hoped-for intercession.", "reasons": "Muqātil connects it to people's hope of angelic intercession. Rāzī relates al-Lāt and al-ʿUzzā's alleged authority to conjecture and desire and says 53:26 answers their supposed intercession. Ibn ʿĀshūr says 53:24's denial leads naturally to the idolaters' claims in 39:3 and 10:18 and then the serious matter of intercession. Study Quran describes the sūra's second section as rebuking Quraysh's idol worship, ignorance, conjecture, and appeal to angels. Islahi says idolaters follow baseless wishes despite clear guidance; Study Quran says their adapted god and hereafter effectively deny divine mastery."}, {"id": "53:25/q12/p2", "position": "It warns that selecting a desired deity cannot evade punishment in this life or the next.", "reasons": "Rāzī offers this explanation and reads the next verse, 53:26, as confirming that intercession will not avail."}, {"id": "53:25/q12/p3", "position": "It consoles the Prophet that deniers remain under God's power despite rejecting his message.", "reasons": "Rāzī offers this after noting that Muhammad had explained his mission and divine unity without winning their belief."}, {"id": "53:25/q12/p4", "position": "It concludes the preceding proof of revelation and divine unity by confirming resurrection.", "reasons": "Rāzī takes established revelation, including 53:4, as warrant for trusting Muhammad's report of resurrection; God's ownership of both lives closes the proof."}, {"id": "53:25/q12/p5", "position": "It replies to the claim that believers' poverty shows they are not better guided.", "reasons": "Rāzī cites the unbelievers' claim in 46:11 and answers that God gives wealth and guidance as He wills in either life."}]}
{"id": "53:25/q13", "question": "What is reported to have happened during the public recitation tied to this passage?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "53:25/q13/p1", "position": "Satan inserted praise of the exalted cranes; Meccan polytheists hoped for intercession, and both groups prostrated at the sūra's end for different objects.", "reasons": "Muqātil says the phrase was put on Muhammad's tongue, making polytheists rejoice over hoped-for angelic intercession. He says Muhammad and believers prostrated to affirm God, polytheists at their idols, and the elderly Walīd ibn al-Mughīra lifted dirt to his forehead in prostration."}]}
{"id": "53:25/q14", "question": "What follows from God's superiority over creatures for the claim that He has children?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "53:25/q14/p1", "position": "If offspring were possible, God would have a stronger claim to sons than the polytheists, though He is exalted above offspring.", "reasons": "Māwardī reasons from God's greater power over created beings while expressly distancing Him from the claim."}]}
{"id": "53:25/q15", "question": "What grounds temporal priority and posteriority?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "53:25/q15/p1", "position": "Temporal order has reality through God; without Him there would be no before or after.", "reasons": "Rāzī cites, without grading, the Prophet's saying 'Do not revile time, for time is God' and argues that God grounds the temporal order that people would otherwise revile."}]}
{"id": "53:25/q16", "question": "Who is addressed by the warning that wishes cannot override God's rule?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "53:25/q16/p1", "position": "Every individual, including members of later religious communities.", "reasons": "Islahi says the general 'man' of 53:24 has no exception. He names Arabs, Jews, Christians, and Muslims; he connects Jewish and Christian amāniyyu to al-Baqarah and Āl ʿImrān and says Muslims too devised beliefs contrary to Qur'an and Sunnah by following them. Desires do not alter reality or bias divine law."}]}
{"id": "53:32/q01", "question": "How does “those who avoid” attach to the preceding verse?", "turns_on": "Whether the relative phrase continues the description of good-doers or starts a new predication.", "positions": [{"id": "53:32/q01/p1", "position": "It qualifies or substitutes for the previous “those who do good.”", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya calls it an adjective; Rāzī prefers a badal, as avoiding major sins identifies the good-doers. Al-Samīn and al-Ālūsī allow apposition or clarification; Ibn ʿĀshūr makes it a defining modifier."}, {"id": "53:32/q01/p2", "position": "It begins a new sentence or is raised as praise.", "reasons": "Rāzī says the new sentence promises forgiveness to avoiders and distinguishes them from good-doers and unaccountable children. Al-Bayḍāwī, al-Nasafī, al-Samīn and al-Ālūsī allow an omitted subject, 'they are those who.'"}, {"id": "53:32/q01/p3", "position": "Making “those who” subject and “vast in forgiveness” its predicate is rejected.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī rejects the omitted-link analysis; Saʿdī al-Muftī objects that one approach leaves the earlier phrase idle."}, {"id": "53:32/q01/p4", "position": "Yajtanibūn means to keep away or leave aside.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya supplies the lexical gloss, fitting the description of doers of good."}]}
{"id": "53:32/q02", "question": "What does the present tense of “avoid” convey?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "53:32/q02/p1", "position": "It indicates continuing, habitual avoidance of varied sins.", "reasons": "Rāzī contrasts the past tense for once-for-all repudiation of idols at 39:17 and the present here and at 42:37; Bursevī says purification precedes adornment and repeated restraint merits Paradise; al-Ālūsī concurs."}]}
{"id": "53:32/q03", "question": "What makes a sin a major sin here?", "turns_on": "Which mark of gravity is decisive: explicit threat, legal penalty, religious contempt, repentance, or shirk.", "positions": [{"id": "53:32/q03/p1", "position": "A specific severe threat of punishment marks major sin.", "reasons": "Muqātil and Ibn ʿAbbās specify the Fire; Bayḍāwī, Biqāʿī, Bursawī, Ibn ʿĀshūr and others use explicit grave warning. Al-Ālūsī prefers threat over hadd alone because it captures slander, tale-bearing, and filial disobedience."}, {"id": "53:32/q03/p2", "position": "It is shirk or unbelief, the supreme great sin.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī is reported by Māwardī; Zayd b. Aslam explains singular kabīr as kufr; Ibn ʿAbbās explains the singular as shirk; Qushayrī calls shirk greatest of all."}, {"id": "53:32/q03/p3", "position": "A sin not expiated without repentance is major.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĪsā, the Muʿtazila as Rāzī and Abū Ḥayyān report, and Zamakhsharī in Study Quran use this criterion. Rāzī rejects it as unclear; Abū Ḥayyān calls it a Muʿtazilite tendency. Abū Ḥayyān reiterates that Zamakhsharī's repentance-only account reflects Muʿtazilite doctrine."}, {"id": "53:32/q03/p4", "position": "A sin becomes major through persistence; repentance removes that status.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās says no major sin remains with seeking forgiveness and no minor with persistence; Ibn Jubayr says no repentance makes a sin major; Biqāʿī cites 24:15 for treating minor wrongdoing lightly."}, {"id": "53:32/q03/p5", "position": "It is a sin with a prescribed worldly penalty.", "reasons": "Jurists in Māwardī, Bayḍāwī, and Ālūsī give the hadd criterion; al-Rāfiʿī leans to it. The position differs from the view that legal penalties define fawāḥish."}, {"id": "53:32/q03/p6", "position": "It bears a hadd, Hell threat, curse, comparable harm, or evident contempt for religion.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya prefers a broad warning/penalty/curse test; Māwardī says hadd or threat. Al-Barīzī's broader test, including apparent wrongful killing or adultery in mistaken belief, is preferred by al-Ālūsī."}, {"id": "53:32/q03/p7", "position": "A sin shows disregard for religion or weak religious commitment.", "reasons": "Rāzī makes social judgment of reverence contextual: a scholar's conduct, a peddler's conduct, and the time of prayer can change gravity. Imām al-Ḥaramayn defines grave offenses by contempt; al-Adhraʿī relates this to probity."}, {"id": "53:32/q03/p8", "position": "Its boundary is intentionally unknown or only approximate.", "reasons": "Al-Wāḥidī says concealment discourages people from treating unlisted acts lightly, likening it to the hidden greatest name, middle prayer, Night of Decree, and response hour. Ibn Ḥajar says proposed tests approximate."}, {"id": "53:32/q03/p9", "position": "The Prophet identified shirk, killing a child for fear of food, and adultery with a neighbor's wife.", "reasons": "Māwardī transmits Ibn Masʿūd's report of the Prophet's examples; the neighbor aggravation also appears in Qāḍī Ḥusayn's view."}, {"id": "53:32/q03/p10", "position": "Ithm is wrongdoing that impedes reward, including oppression and usurping rights.", "reasons": "Rāghib's root gloss is reported by Ṭabāṭabāʾī; Islahi uses the term for rights, injustice and oppression."}, {"id": "53:32/q03/p11", "position": "An explicit Quranic prohibition identifies major sins.", "reasons": "An unnamed definition in Ālūsī also counts hadd, missed immediate obligation, false testimony and perjury; another lists carrion, pork, orphan property and fleeing battle, but critics reject a restricted count. Harawī and Shurayḥ add opposing consensus."}, {"id": "53:32/q03/p12", "position": "Deeming the act lawful would amount to unbelief.", "reasons": "Rāzī reports this criterion but rejects it with other definitions as clarifying an unclear term by an equally unclear one."}, {"id": "53:32/q03/p13", "position": "Kabāʾir is a feminine adj

{"id": "53:32/q04", "question": "How many major sins are there?", "turns_on": "Whether the reports enumerate a fixed prophetic set, a much larger range, or only examples.", "positions": [{"id": "53:32/q04/p1", "position": "Seven destructive sins are singled out.", "reasons": "The hadith names shirk, magic, murder, orphan property, usury, desertion, and slander of chaste believing women; the majority in Ibn ʿAṭiyya and ʿAlī, ʿAṭāʾ and ʿUbayd in Ālūsī cite seven."}, {"id": "53:32/q04/p2", "position": "They are nearer seventy than seven.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās gives this estimate, with Bursevī also quoting it."}, {"id": "53:32/q04/p3", "position": "They are nearer seven hundred than seven.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās is also reported with this larger count; Māwardī and Ālūsī add his maxim about repentance and persistence."}, {"id": "53:32/q04/p4", "position": "Seventeen are counted by bodily or spiritual organ.", "reasons": "Abū Ṭālib al-Makkī counts four of the heart, four tongue, three belly, two sexual, two hand, flight from battle, and filial disobedience; Ālūsī notes flaws."}, {"id": "53:32/q04/p5", "position": "Twenty-five explicit hadith cases are counted.", "reasons": "Al-ʿAlāʾī gives twenty-five, but Ibn Ḥajar criticizes omissions."}, {"id": "53:32/q04/p6", "position": "Other counts are three, four, ten, fourteen, or fifteen.", "reasons": "Ālūsī reports these alternatives, including three from Ibn Masʿūd."}, {"id": "53:32/q04/p7", "position": "Ibn ʿAbbās counts sins named through Qurʾān 4:31.", "reasons": "The report covers the opening of al-Nisāʾ through its major-sins verse."}]}
{"id": "53:32/q05", "question": "Does the verse distinguish major from minor sins?", "turns_on": "Whether 'minor' is an absolute category or a relative description before God, and what avoiding major sins guarantees.", "positions": [{"id": "53:32/q05/p1", "position": "Sins divide into major and minor, with lesser sins pardoned on avoiding major ones.", "reasons": "Ṭabarī, Naḥḥās, Abū Ḥayyān, Ibn Kathīr and Ṭabāṭabāʾī cite 4:31. Jishumī uses the distinction against Khārijites; al-Ghazālī says denying it is inappropriate; the majority says both sides recognize differences in moral probity."}, {"id": "53:32/q05/p2", "position": "Every sin is major in absolute relation to God's command; lesser is relative.", "reasons": "Qushayrī, Rāzī, Asʾila al-Muqḥima, and scholars named by Ālūsī argue that defying God's gifts makes any sin weighty, though shirk is greatest. Ibn Furak attributes this to Ashʿarites; Ibn Masʿūd reports every prohibition as major. Error and forgetfulness receive grace."}, {"id": "53:32/q05/p3", "position": "Avoiding major sins merits forgiveness as a divine promise.", "reasons": "Jishumī says pardon is deserved and supports the doctrine of divine threat; Ṭabarī cites 4:31, whereas Bayḍāwī and Nasafī emphasize God's freedom to forgive as He wills."}]}
{"id": "53:32/q06", "question": "How is “major sins” read?", "turns_on": "Whether the singular denotes a collective genus or a single supreme sin; readers and grammatical precedents vary.", "positions": [{"id": "53:32/q06/p1", "position": "The singular kabīr al-ithm is read, expressing a genus, multiple sins, or shirk.", "reasons": "Farrāʾ names Yaḥyā and Ibn Masʿūd's companions; Ḥamza, Kisāʾī, and Khalaf recur. Al-Fārisī argues faʿīl can be collective like faʿūl, citing 4:92, 6:112, 26:100–101, 4:69, 50:17 and poetry; the abstract ithm is collective. Sources differ on exact reader lists."}, {"id": "53:32/q06/p2", "position": "The plural kabāʾir is the majority reading.", "reasons": "It directly expresses multiple grave sins; al-Wāḥidī notes singular ithm can still denote a mass or genus. Ibn ʿĀshūr calls the singular/plural alternation compatible with a collective noun."}]}
{"id": "53:32/q07", "question": "What are the fawāḥish?", "turns_on": "Whether the word denotes all ugly sins, a legally punished class, or sexual offenses in particular.", "positions": [{"id": "53:32/q07/p1", "position": "They are especially ugly or manifestly shameful grave sins.", "reasons": "Ṭabrisī calls them the ugliest; Rāzī derives manifest repugnance from Arabic and camel usage; Rāghib and Ibn al-Jawzī attest the root's excess and foul speech. Ibn ʿĀshūr gives adultery, theft and ambush killing; Ṭabāṭabāʾī adduces adultery and sodomy."}, {"id": "53:32/q07/p2", "position": "They are acts carrying a prescribed worldly penalty.", "reasons": "Muqātil and Ibn ʿAbbās distinguish Hell-marked major sins from legally punished indecencies; later sources repeat this. The Nabhan chronology raises a Meccan/Medinan problem."}, {"id": "53:32/q07/p3", "position": "They mean adultery or illicit intercourse.", "reasons": "Zayd b. Aslam, Māwardī, Qurṭubī and Islahi identify zina or open sexual transgression; Ibn al-Jawzī supplies 3:135, 4:15, 7:33 and 33:30 as usage."}, {"id": "53:32/q07/p4", "position": "They mean all sin or disobedience.", "reasons": "Māwardī and Qushayrī report the broad gloss; Ibn al-Jawzī cites 7:28 for sin. Zayd b. Thābit emphasizes both outward and inward indecencies."}, {"id": "53:32/q07/p5", "position": "The term can designate sodomy or a wife's marital misconduct elsewhere.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Jawzī adduces Lot's people at 29:28 for the former, and 4:19 and 65:1 for the latter; these are Quranic usages of the word."}, {"id": "53:32/q07/p6", "position": "These are the sins already mentioned in the surrounding description.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya ties them to the prior discussion rather than listing individual acts."}]}
{"id": "53:32/q08", "question": "Why mention fawāḥish after major sins?", "turns_on": "Whether coordination selects a heinous subset, marks overlapping categories, or repeats a synonym.", "positions": [{"id": "53:32/q08/p1", "position": "Fawāḥish are a specially heinous subset of major sins, named after the general category.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥayyān and Bursawī call it specific after general; Bayḍāwī and Nasafī say particularly obscene members; Rāzī distinguishes magnitude from conspicuous ugliness, explaining why only kabāʾir needs 'of sin.'"}, {"id": "53:32/q08/p2", "position": "They are coordinated, overlapping but distinguishable categories.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr says the conjunction marks distinct categories despite overlap; Rāzī contrasts quantitative greatness and qualitative ugliness."}, {"id": "53:32/q08/p3", "position": "They may be synonyms for grave sins.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī reports this alternative."}]}

{"id": "53:32/q10", "question": "What does the Arabic root of lamam suggest?", "turns_on": "Whether the root's operative nuance is nearness, smallness, or brief occurrence.", "positions": [{"id": "53:32/q10/p1", "position": "It suggests a brief, occasional visit or lapse without lasting involvement.", "reasons": "Jarīr, Aʿshā, Umayya and anonymous poetry illustrate passing visits; Mujāhid reports pilgrims' refrain 'what servant has not slipped.' Zajjāj, Farrāʾ, Baghawī and Niftawayh draw the nonhabitual sense. A Prophetic quotation of the couplet is reported, though Ibn Kathīr questions its elevation."}, {"id": "53:32/q10/p2", "position": "It suggests slight contact, coming near, or almost doing an act.", "reasons": "Farrāʾ cites a near-fatal blow; Mubarrad cites near-death, a palm near fruiting, and a lock near the ear; Abū Zayd, Azharī and Jawharī provide approximation. {"id": "53:32/q11", "question": "How does the exception “except al-lamam” work?", "turns_on": "Whether lamam belongs to the preceding class, lies outside it, or is joined by an adjectival/conjunctive parse.", "positions": [{"id": "53:32/q11/p1", "position": "It is disconnected: minor lapses are outside major sins and fawāḥish.", "reasons": "Abū ʿUbayda's gazelle-and-camel analogy and Ṭabarī's 4:31 argument support it; most grammarians and commentators take this route. Naḥḥās says al-lamam is accusative as a heterogeneous exception. Wāḥidī prefers it because a connected exception might imply permission. Abū ʿUbayd permits a pause before it."}, {"id": "53:32/q11/p2", "position": "It is connected: a person can lapse into a grave sin, then repent.", "reasons": "Ṭabarī, Thaʿlabī and Baghawī transmit it from Ibn ʿAbbās, Abū Hurayra, Mujāhid and Ḥasan. Ibn al-Jawzī makes the pre-Islam and repentant-grave-sin readings connected. Rāzī says all disobedience is grave relative to God, so some is excepted by grace."}, {"id": "53:32/q11/p3", "position": "Illā functions adjectivally as “other than.”", "reasons": "Rāzī and Abū Ḥayyān compare 21:22; al-Samīn and al-Ālūsī discuss grammatical definiteness and Ibn al-Ḥājib's restriction. Ālūsī says Sibawayh allows it more broadly but finds it unlikely here."}, {"id": "53:32/q11/p4", "position": "The exception is connected because lamam is lesser yet remains within the genus of sins.", "reasons": "Ṭabrisī expressly calls it an accusative exception from sins and indecencies, although lesser."}, {"id": "53:32/q11/p5", "position": "It attaches to the implied action of avoidance.", "reasons": "Rāzī construes it as 'they avoid sins except approaching them without doing them.'"}, {"id": "53:32/q11/p6", "position": "Illā was proposed as “and,” but that is rejected.", "reasons": "Farrāʾ rejects this reading and understands lamam as sins approaching minor offenses."}, {"id": "53:32/q11/p7", "position": "A pause before the exception depends on whether it is syntactically detached.", "reasons": "Abū ʿUbayd permits a pause for disconnected exceptions; another view bars stopping before an accusative substitute tied to its antecedent, though nominative may permit it."}]}
{"id": "53:32/q12", "question": "What is encompassed by God's vast forgiveness?", "turns_on": "Whether forgiveness is promised through avoidance of major sins, conditioned on repentance, or left to God's will.", "positions": [{"id": "53:32/q12/p1", "position": "Minor sins are pardoned for those avoiding major sins.", "reasons": "Ṭabarī and others use 4:31; Ibn ʿAbbās says prayers expiate lapses below the two punishments. Ibn ʿAṭiyya says this promise consoles believers, who commonly lapse."}, {"id": "53:32/q12/p2", "position": "God forgives repentant grave sinners as well as lesser lapses.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās applies vast forgiveness to a repentant lapse; Ibn Kathīr cites 39:53; Rāzī says the breadth embraces repentant major sinners but persistent sinners lie outside the stated pardon. {"id": "53:32/q13", "question": "Why call the forgiveness “vast” and God “your Lord”?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "53:32/q13/p1", "position": "“Vast” metaphorically conveys abundance, and “your Lord” conveys care.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr compares 40:7, notes the Prophet is addressed as the channel of care for followers, and links the breadth to allowing lapses among righteous people."}]}
{"id": "53:32/q14", "question": "What does God's knowing people from their origin establish?", "turns_on": "Whether the creation reminder chiefly establishes foreknowledge, hidden knowledge, resurrection, or compassionate awareness of weakness.", "positions": [{"id": "53:32/q14/p1", "position": "God has known every person's deeds, inward state, and ultimate destiny since before birth.", "reasons": "Ṭabarī specifies believer/unbeliever, good/evil and obedient/disobedient; Ḥasan says He knows what each will do and become. {"id": "53:32/q22", "question": "When may a person praise or commend someone?", "turns_on": "How certainty, audience, motive, and legal or public need qualify praise.", "positions": [{"id": "53:32/q22/p1", "position": "Truthful, qualified commendation for a public or legal need is allowed.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya permits commending a model and assessing witnesses; Abū Ḥayyān and Ālūsī allow testimony establishing rights.
